title.en: The Fourteen Thousand: Khara and Dushana
title.zh: 一萬四千：伽羅與毒夏那

region.zh: 閻那私陀那，德干森林（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Aranya Kanda, Khara-Dushana battle

summary.en: Sent by Ravana to avenge his sister's humiliation, the rakshasa lord Khara brought fourteen thousand warriors against three exiles and a hermitage. Rama sent his brother and wife to a cave and met the army alone; the battle is the epic's demonstration-piece - one archer erasing a host - and its victory was so complete that Surpanakha had to carry the news to Lanka herself.
summary.zh: 奉羅波那之命為其妹受辱復仇的羅剎王伽羅，率一萬四千戰士對抗三位流亡者與一處仙居。羅摩遣弟與妻入洞穴，獨自迎戰大軍；此戰是史詩的示範之作——一名射手抹去一支軍隊——而其勝利如此徹底，以致首哩薄那迦只能親自將消息帶回楞伽。

passages.text: Khara's arithmetic was imperial: fourteen thousand against two brothers and a woman - the calculus of Rakshasa power applied to a hermitage. Rama's answer was a tactical poem: wife and brother in a cave, a single bow in the clearing, and the forest's terror met one man at a time until the column was spent. The hermitage resumed its fires by evening; the war that followed was not Lanka's choice but its sister's report - the report of a battle that had gone entirely the wrong way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

region.zh: 溫迪亞海岸（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Kishkindha Kanda, Sampati episode

summary.en: The search parties had exhausted the south - until a huge old vulture dropped from a crag with his wings burned away. Sampati, brother of Jatayu, had once spread his wings to shield his brother from the sun and lost his sight; hearing Rama's name, he regained one eye by merit - and gave the monkeys the intelligence that ended the search: she is in Lanka, in the Ashoka grove.
summary.zh: 南方搜索各隊已至山窮水盡——直至一隻巨齒老鷹自崖壁墜下，雙翼焦黑。商波底，闍吒優私之兄，曾展翼為弟擋日而失明；聽聞羅摩之名，憑功德復得一眼——並把終結搜索的情報交予猴族：她在楞伽，在無憂林苑。

passages.text: The vulture's history was a service record: wings burned in a brother's shadow, years of blindness in the crag - and a rumor of Rama's name in the monkey-chorus below. At the name his one blind eye cleared: the merit of a lifetime's shielding paid out at the moment the shield's cause needed him - the epic's economy of sacrifice made literal. His intelligence was the war's first map: Lanka's shore, the grove, the tower where she sat - the brothers' search ended with a bird's report and began the campaign.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.zh: 黎什耶施陵伽：司雨仙人

region.zh: 鴦伽邊境森林（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Bala Kanda, Rishyashringa episode

summary.en: A seer's son raised in the forest seeing no one but his father had never known a woman - and his purity worked like weather: wherever he sat, the rain came. The kingdom in drought sent courtesans to fetch him; the innocent was led to Ayodhya, married to the king's daughter, and officiated at the sacrifice that gave Dasharatha his four sons - the epic's own fertility-plot as ritual technology.
summary.zh: 一位仙人之子在林中長大，除父之外從未見過女人——其純潔如天氣般生效：他坐於何處，雨即降於何處。苦旱之國遣妓者前去迎接；天真的仙人被引至阿逾陀，與公主成婚，並主持了賜予十車王四子的祭祀——史詩自身以儀式技術呈現的生育情節。

passages.text: The boy in the forest had never seen a city, a crowd, or a woman; his innocence was the instrument: rain followed him like a reputation. The drought-king's solution was a embassy of courtesans: the seduction was conducted with such tact that the innocent followed them to the city thinking it hospitality. Married into Ayodhya's house, he presided over the putrakameshti; the four princes of the epic are, in one reading, the rain he carried with him - a fertility-rite retold as a dynasty's founding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.zh: 陀羅於婆黎屍前之哀歌

region.zh: 猴國吉什金陀（象徵性定位於漢皮）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Kishkindha Kanda, Tara's lament

summary.en: When the hidden arrow brought down the monkey-king Vali, his queen Tara ran to the field and found a war's worth of sense in her grief: she argued with Sugriva for the crown, with the dying king for forgiveness, and finally with Rama himself - the epic's sharpest woman's speech, delivered over a corpse. Her counsel 'to whom will you be loyal now?' shaped the alliance that won Lanka.
summary.zh: 暗箭擊落猴王婆黎時，王后陀羅奔至戰場，在悲慟中說出一場戰爭份量的道理：她向須羯哩婆爭王位，向垂死的王爭諒解，最後與羅摩本人辯論——史詩中最鋒利的女性言辭，於一具屍體前講出。她那句『你如今將忠於誰？』塑造了後來贏得楞伽的同盟。

passages.text: Tara reached the fallen king before his breath ended, and her lament was argument: on the arrow, on the code, on the politics of a kingdom where kings fall by other people's wars. To the dying Vali she gave the only mercy that mattered - forgiveness of Sugriva, sworn in his own mouth - and to the new king a constitution: the brother you feared is now your ally; govern like it. Her audience with Rama ended the interrogation the epic still conducts: the queen of the victim interrogating the ideal king - and receiving, for once, an answer that admits the cost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.en: Vishvamitra's Weapons: The Arsenal of Sound
title.zh: 維什瓦米陀的武器：以音聲傳遞的武庫

region.zh: 丹陀迦森林（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Bala Kanda, the celestial weapons

summary.en: After Tataka's fall, the seer Vishvamitra gave Rama a graduation gift: the names of the weapons. Each one spoken - the dart of wind, the noose of death, the discus, the fire-missile - arrived in the prince's hand fully armed, personified, and obedient. The arsenal was an curriculum in sound: the Vedic theology that power is a name, correctly pronounced.
summary.zh: 多吒迦授首之後，仙人維什瓦米陀贈予羅摩一份畢業禮：武器之名。每一個被誦出的名字——風之鏢、死之索、法輪、火矢——便全副武裝、人格化、馴順地落於王子掌中。武庫即一門關於聲音的課程：吠陀神學——力量是一個正確發音的名字。

passages.text: The teacher's gift was a vocabulary: each weapon had a name, a family, a temperament - and arrived when called, like staff at a king's court. The prince received them as gifts of speech: the wind-missile, the death-noose, the discus of the sun - each personified and each addressed by name before it flew. The scene is the Vedic word-theology staged: in this tradition the correct name is the technology - pronunciation as empowerment, the boy's mouth armed like a smithy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.en: Bharata's Four-Week Search for His Brother
title.zh: 婆羅多為尋兄而行的四週之旅

region.zh: 自阿逾陀出發的林路（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Ramayana of Valmiki, oldest strata c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE (Griffith translation, 1870-74)

source.work: The Ramayan of Valmiki, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1870-74), Ayodhya Kanda, Bharata's search

summary.en: Bharata, refusing a throne he had never asked for, took the army on a month-long walk across the forests to find Rama and return everything: the crown, the mother's crime, the city's grief. The search visits hermitage after hermitage - a survey of the forest's saints, each of whom tells the prince what renunciation looks like from inside - until at Chitrakuta the brothers meet and the regency begins.
summary.zh: 拒絕一個從未求取的王位的婆羅多，率軍隊徒步月餘跨越森林尋找羅摩，要把一切歸還：王冠、母親之罪、城市之哀。此行遍訪一處又一處仙居——對森林聖者的巡禮，每位都告訴王子出離從內部看來是什麼模樣——直到質多羅俱吒兄弟重逢，攝政始焉。

passages.text: The prince's march was a refusal with logistics: an army behind him, a crown in his hand, and a single sentence to his guides - take me to the man who should be wearing this. The hermitages on the road became the syllabus: each sage received the heir and taught him what he was refusing to be - a tour of the forest's philosophy by its most reluctant student. At Chitrakuta the brothers' meeting is the epic's political heart: the crown offered, the exile refused, and the sandals that would govern in place of a king - the state run by a proxy promise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Griffith 1870-74); not verbatim.

title.en: The Birth of Ganesha and the Elephant's Head

region.zh: 吉羅娑，濕婆居所（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Puranic cycle, retold in Donald A. Mackenzie, Indian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. VIII (public domain)

source.work: Indian Myth and Legend, by Donald A. Mackenzie (1913), ch. VIII

summary.en: Parvati, wanting a doorkeeper loyal to herself, made a boy from her own body's scurf and set him at the bath-house door. Shiva, returning unannounced, was refused - and struck the boy's head off. The mother's grief forced the repair: the first head available, an elephant's, was set on the child, and Ganesha - remover of obstacles, patron of beginnings - was complete, with a broken tusk for a pen.
summary.zh: 波羅婆蒂欲得一名忠於己的守門人，以身之垢造一男孩，置於浴場之門。未經通報歸來的濕婆被拒於門外——怒斬童首。母親之悲迫使修復：就近可得的頭是一枚象首，於是移除障礙者、開端之神甘尼薩完具，並以斷牙為筆。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Ganesha Chaturthi); source is a public-domain scholarly retelling, not a primary translation; recorded as such. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: The mother's craft was housework raised to cosmology: a boy made of the scurf of her skin, posted at her bath's door with orders that outranked the husband's. Shiva's sentries were not consulted: refused at the door of his own house, the god took the boy's head in one stroke - the familiar tragedy of a rule nobody had been told about. The repair was the myth's making: the elephant's head, the vow of precedece (worshipped before all gods), the broken tusk - the elephant-boy became the god of every beginning and the breaker of every obstacle.
passages.note: Retold from Mackenzie, Indian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. VIII; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Retold in English by Donald A. Mackenzie, 1913 (public domain)

title.zh: 克里希那對難敵的最後警告

texts.period: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Udyoga Parva, Krishna and Duryodhana

summary.en: Before the cosmic form, Krishna made one last private appeal in Duryodhana's own terms: the five brothers had earned peace, the elders had begged for it, the kingdom was bigger than one man's envy - and the tyrant answered with a kidnapping plot for the envoy himself. Krishna rose from his seat and left the court a prophecy: the war is now yours, and your name will be its synonym.
summary.zh: 在宇宙之形之前，克里希那以難敵自己的語言作最後一次私下的懇求：五兄弟已求得和平，長者已為之懇請，王國大於一人之妒——而暴君竟以綁架使者的陰謀作答。克里希那起身離廷，留下預言：戰爭如今屬於你，而你的名字將成為它的同義詞。

passages.text: The last appeal was framed as business: the elders' wish, the army's cost, five villages against an age's ruin - the envoy speaking the tyrant's own arithmetic. The answer was a plot against the envoy: seize Krishna, said the prince - and the court's oldest men stood up against their own heir for the first time. The prophecy on his way out was the age's epitaph drafted early: the name Duryodhana would stand for the whole catastrophe - the epic's naming of a man as an era's mistake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.
